newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH C.BANK SAYS CROWN DEVAL NO EXPORT PANACEA.
newsitem.headline: CZECH C.BANK SAYS CROWN DEVAL NO EXPORT PANACEA.

text.p: The Czech central bank (CNB) said on Wednesday that a devaluation of the crown would not provide a significant boost to exports.

"The main exporters in the Czech Republic don't confirm that the devaluation of the crown would help them to increase exports...Devaluation or exchange rate change wouldn't be the best medicine," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters.

The Czech crown weakened in morning trading with dealers blaming televised comments by the director of the National Economics Institute Jan Svejnar late on Tuesday that the crown should be gradually devalued to help exports.
The crown was fixed at 29.072 to the dollar and 17.277 to the mark putting it 1.82 percent above the mid-point of its mar/dollar basket. The crown opened at around 2.3 perecnt above the midpoint.
Immediately after the CNB comments the crown recovered to close to its opening level.

Svejnar, one of the most respected economists in the country, based his recommendations for a devaluation on the argument that the crown was undergoing a real appreciation against its main trading partners because of higher consumer price inflation in the Czech Republic.

Svehla said the central bank understood Svejnar's argument but believed that the producer price index, which is rising at around half the rate of consumer inflation, was a more important indicator of export competitiveness.
"If we base this comparison (with western countries) on the level of PPI the real appreciation (of the crown) is not as fast as one could think on the basis of CPI," said Svehla.
PPI is running at a yearly rate of around four percent compared with eight percent for CPI, Svehla said.
The Czech trade deficit was approximately $5.5 billion in 1996 and was $469 million for the month of January, at Wednesday's exchange rate.

The Czech Republic's current account ended 1996 with a deficit of $4.476 billion, compared to a $1.362 billion shortfall in 1995, the central bank said on Tuesday. Foreign exchange reserves are still healthy, it added.
